Revised assessment with literature context:
The statement balances strong labor conditions with below-target inflation and soft business investment, and pairs a 25 bp cut with an early end to balance-sheet runoff—netting a cautiously dovish tone. In New Keynesian models with nominal rigidities, expected inflation and credibility are central (Woodford), so low market- and survey-based inflation expectations justify easier policy to re-anchor inflation at the symmetric 2% objective. An inflation-forecast-targeting lens (Svensson) similarly supports preemptive easing when expectations are drifting low. While unemployment is low, the long-run neutrality view (Friedman, Phelps) cautions against relying on a permanent inflation–unemployment trade-off, reinforcing the focus on price stability rather than “overheating” labor markets. The observed softness in business fixed investment is consistent with evidence that investment—particularly inventories—is sensitive to internal funds and credit conditions (Kashyap, Lamont, and Stein, 1994), and with broader agency-cost channels that amplify weakness (Gertler), both of which are mitigated by lower policy rates and supportive liquidity via reinvestments. The IOER adjustment and earlier conclusion of balance-sheet runoff reinforce transmission without signaling aggressive easing. Two hawkish dissents temper the dovish tilt. Net: supportive of continued expansion but mindful of inflation undershoot and global risks—cautiously positive rather than outright upbeat.

Adjusted sentiment (more dovish given inflation shortfall and soft capex, but moderated by strong labor and dissents): sentiment score = 0.15
